750a5d97-2f76-4e8f-afce-54809973139c.body:
Short version: as an EU citizen, the EHIC covers you for temporary stays, but for a multi-year study programme with compulsory hotel internships, you almost certainly need to be insured under KVG — and your school's admissions office is right to say so.

The exemption route exists (Art. 3 KVG exemption for people with foreign insurance), but it's narrower than most students think:

1) **Who processes the exemption** — the cantonal health authorities (in Vaud, the SVD — Service de la santé publique) decide on exemptions from compulsory KVG insurance. The insurer processes the actual policy. The exemption is not something SEM or your hotel employer handles. You apply to the cantonal authority, and you need to prove you have coverage from home that's comparable and that you're not exercising a gainful activity in Switzerland.

2) **Is the EHIC valid for a multi-year programme including internships?** — Here's the catch: the EHIC is meant for temporary stays, not as a substitute for residence-based coverage. Once you're working — and a compulsory hotel internship, even unpaid or low-paid, counts as gainful activity for insurance purposes — the EHIC generally no longer suffices, and you fall under compulsory KVG insurance. That's exactly the scenario your admissions office is warning about. A student who does no work at all and stays under the exemption threshold might scrape by on EHIC for a year, but the moment you're on a hotel payroll, you're on the hook.

3) **Do you need Swiss insurance for the permit even if exempt?** — If you're exempt, you don't need Swiss coverage. But in practice, for a multi-year stay with internships, most EU students end up needing Swiss cover anyway, so the exemption rarely survives contact with the real programme schedule.

4) **What happens if your home cover lapses mid-semester?** — That's the worst case. If your EHIC stops being valid (e.g. your home-country policy lapses) and you're working in Switzerland, you're uninsured — which is both a legal problem and a financial one, since a hospital bill without cover in Switzerland can run into five figures. Don't let a gap happen. If you're even slightly unsure, get Swiss cover.

**Practical next step:** talk to the admissions office or the cantonal SVD in Montreux about an exemption *before* you arrive, in writing. If they confirm you need KVG (most likely, given the internships), then budget for it now: a young-adult basic plan with a high franchise and a Telmed/HMO model runs roughly CHF 250-320/month. If they grant an exemption, keep the confirmation letter safe — you'll need it if a hotel HR ever questions your insurance status.

f1ec9a0c-7b8f-436b-a81f-77b726297b13.body:
Straight answer: Swisscare is not a scam, and it's not 'special school insurance' either — it's a regular KVG-compliant insurer (it underwrites through a Swiss insurance partner) that markets hard to international students. But that doesn't mean it's the cheapest for you.

1) **Does Swisscare stay competitive over a full 4-year degree?** — Its premiums are set for the international-student segment and they do reprice each year like everyone else. The honest answer is you should compare it to a regular KVG policy at *every* renewal, because prices move year to year and your age band shifts. What Swisscare buys you is convenience and English-speaking support, not guaranteed value.

2) **Does it count as compulsory Swiss insurance?** — Yes. A Swisscare basic plan satisfies KVG and covers the same compulsory services as any other insurer's basic plan. You do not need a separate exemption certificate if you hold a Swisscare KVG policy — it *is* your Swiss insurance.

3) **How smooth are real claims?** — This is where it varies. People report fine experiences with routine claims (GP visits, prescriptions). The complaints you see online tend to involve hospital stays and reimbursements where documentation gets sent back and forth. The pragmatic advice: whatever insurer you choose, keep every invoice, and submit claims promptly. Claim smoothness is more about your paperwork than the insurer.

4) **Can you switch from Swisscare to a regular insurer?** — Yes, and it's easy if you do it right. In Switzerland you can change basic insurers twice a year, with a notice period (usually by end of November for January, or end of May for July). Coverage is continuous — no penalty, no health questions for the basic plan. So the low-risk play is: start with whatever covers you now, and switch at the next window if a regular insurer quotes clearly cheaper for the same model and franchise.

**Bottom line:** don't let the school's default choice be your default choice. Use priminfo.admin.ch (the official comparator) and a commercial one like Comparis, quote the *same* deductible and model, and pick on price + support language. The CHF 30-50/month you might save is real money over four years.

af9816a6-ac83-415e-ab76-bafb72fe375d.body:
Good question, and the answer genuinely surprises most students: **international students can qualify for Prämienverbilligung**, but it depends on your canton, your residency status, and above all your income — and your part-time work can absolutely disqualify or qualify you depending on the numbers.

1) **Do international students qualify?** — Yes, in principle. Prämienverbilligung is means-tested, not citizenship-tested. What matters is that you're resident in the canton, subject to compulsory KVG insurance, and your taxable income (plus assets) is below the canton's threshold. Non-EU students are not automatically excluded. Each canton publishes its own income limits and they differ a lot.

2) **Which office do you apply to?** — In Vaud, you apply to the SVA (Caisse de compensation) — specifically their Prämienverbilligung service. In most cantons it's the SVA/AVS office or the cantonal health insurance office, not the tax authority directly. Look for 'Prämienverbilligung' (IP — Indemnités pour frais de primes) on your canton's health services page.

3) **Does part-time internship income count?** — Yes, your income from the weekend barman shifts and any internship pay counts toward the threshold. This cuts both ways: a small income can push you *below* the limit (good), but a decent internship salary can push you *over* (bad). It's per calendar year, and cantons look at your income from the whole year, so a six-month paid internship can matter.

4) **Is the reduction retroactive?** — Here's the practical gotcha: you usually receive Prämienverbilligung from the start of the year *if you apply in time*, but many cantons only backdate if you apply before the deadline (often mid-year). Applying late can mean you lose the first months. So apply early — don't wait until after your internship finishes.

**One more thing:** you mentioned 'CHF 300 deductible... thinking of going with a higher franchise' — a higher deductible (Franchise) lowers your monthly premium, which is smart on a student budget, but note Prämienverbilligung is calculated on the *standard* premium, so your IP amount isn't reduced by choosing a high franchise. Take the high franchise, get the reduction, and you've minimised both lines.

**Practical next step:** check your canton's current income threshold (search 'Prämienverbilligung [canton] Grenze 2026'), and if your yearly income is under it, apply now — even mid-year. The form is short and can usually be submitted online.

293b9e8d-0455-46d4-a51c-a9fd4435f9d8.body:
Telmed is the right instinct for a healthy 24-year-old, and here's the detail that makes the choice clearer than the marketing makes it.

1) **Does Telmed actually work at 2am?** — Yes, but with the right expectation. Telmed lines (Medgate is the big one, run by Swiss insurers) are staffed around the clock. The nurse/doctor on the line triages you: if it's a genuine emergency, they tell you to go to the emergency room or call 144; if it's routine, they advise or arrange a GP appointment; and they can often prescribe over the phone. Nobody is left to 'sit and wait with a fever'. What Telmed does *not* do is replace emergency care — it routes you to it. That's exactly what you want: a Sunday-night fever gets a same-hour call, and you only go to the ER if the line tells you to.

2) **Is saving CHF 40-60/month worth it for someone who mainly needs sports injuries?** — This is the key nuance. Managed-care models (Telmed, HMO, family doctor) all gate specialist access through a first contact. For a sports injury, the path is: Telmed call → GP → referral to physio or specialist. In most cases the GP can handle initial assessment and physio referrals directly. So yes, the saving is worth it for most students — the restriction rarely bites for routine and sports care. Where it bites is if you have a chronic condition where you already see a named specialist — then the HMO/family-doctor model adds friction every time.

3) **Which model works for internships abroad?** — Important nuance here: managed-care models apply to care *within Switzerland*. When you're abroad, your KVG basic insurance covers medically necessary emergency care in the EU/EFTA area (and Swiss insurers generally cover worldwide emergencies, though non-EU is usually limited to acute emergencies). The gating restriction doesn't apply abroad — you can see a local doctor directly. So your internship in a European hotel is covered for emergencies regardless of model. For long-term stays abroad you'd want additional travel/liability cover, but that's separate from KVG.

4) **Which quote site is more accurate, priminfo or Comparis?** — Use priminfo.admin.ch as the *authoritative* one: it's the official federal comparator, so the premiums listed are the actual approved ones for your canton, age, and model. Comparis is a commercial broker — it's fine for orientation but it may steer you toward insurers it earns commission from, and its default settings sometimes don't match your exact canton/franchise. My rule: find the cheapest on priminfo, then check whether a Comparis offer for the *same* plan undercuts it before signing.

**Practical next step:** quote the exact same combination — Telmed model, franchise CHF 2,500 (max, cheapest premium), young-adult band (18-25) — on priminfo for your canton and buy the cheapest. You can always switch models at the twice-yearly window if your health situation changes.

d1ca7dd0-a3f5-401c-aba7-e935032b95a7.body:
You're not the first person this happens to, and there's a workable path — but you need to act now, because time is exactly what you don't have.

Here's what's actually true about backdating:

1) **How far past the deadline can an insurer backdate?** — Insurers can generally backdate coverage to your arrival date, but the longer the gap, the harder it gets, and some insurers cap backdating at a few weeks. The law requires you to be insured from arrival; a late application usually triggers a cantonal surcharge on top of premiums, and some cantons add an admin penalty. Practically: if you're past the 3-month mark, the insurer will almost certainly still cover you, but the canton may bill you for the full gap plus a surcharge (often a percentage of the premium).

2) **Fines or warnings?** — This is where it's real: Swiss cantons do check for gaps in compulsory cover, and a confirmed gap can mean a fine. It's usually proportional and not catastrophic, but it's avoidable if you close the gap fast. The damage to your wallet is mostly the retroactive premiums, not the fine.

3) **Who to apply through — Swisscare, a regular insurer, or a broker?** — For a late application, I'd go to a regular insurer directly rather than a broker, because you want the insurer's *underwriting* to see your full situation and give you the backdate in writing. Swisscare is a fine option for international students and handles these cases all the time (late arrivals are its bread and butter), so if speed matters, it's a defensible choice. What matters most: get an application submitted this week, tell them your true arrival date, and ask explicitly for backdated coverage to that date. Get confirmation in writing before you rely on it.

4) **Can you soften the financial hit?** — Yes, two levers. First, choose the cheapest compliant model: highest franchise (CHF 2,500) + Telmed/HMO model — for the retroactive period this reduces what you owe. Second, check whether you qualify for Prämienverbilligung (see the other thread) — if your income is low, the canton may offset part of the retroactive premiums.

**Bottom line:** the goal is to be insured from arrival with the gap as short as possible. Insurers won't refuse to cover you for a late application — they'll just charge you. So stop reading, pick an insurer, and apply this week.

46272a80-5813-4aaf-a418-d161572b601a.body:
This is a very common situation and it has a defined answer — you do NOT need to leave the country, but you DO need to get the paperwork moving before your current permit expires.

1) **Does a mandatory internship automatically extend your student permit?** — A mandatory internship that's part of your diploma is generally treated as an extension of your studies, not a separate work permit. But 'generally' is not 'automatically': your permit's validity dates are tied to your enrolment, and if there's a gap between your official graduation date and the internship start, the cantonal migration office (SEM in the case of non-EU) needs to see that the internship is part of your programme. Some schools handle this by confirming the internship is required for graduation; others don't, which is why you must check with your school's international office in writing.

2) **Who applies — you or the hotel?** — Both, in different ways. You apply to extend/update your residence permit with the cantonal migration office. The hotel provides a contract and may need to confirm employment, but for a mandatory internship the *school* is the key actor: they confirm the internship is required for your degree. So your first move is the school's international office, not HR.

3) **What happens during the gap month?** — You're allowed to remain in Switzerland while an application is pending — you don't have to leave and re-enter. The catch: you can't *start working* until the permit is updated. So if the hotel needs you on day one and your permit still says 'student until X', that's a problem the school and hotel need to solve together, usually by having the school issue a letter confirming the internship and the migration office issuing a temporary permit confirmation.

4) **The actual timeline** — Realistically: a few weeks for the school to issue the confirmation, then 2-6 weeks for the cantonal office to process, depending on the canton and workload. That's why you must start now, even though the internship is two months away. The single worst thing you can do is wait until a month before, because then the paperwork queue owns your timeline.

**Practical next step:** this week, email your school's international office with: your graduation date, the internship contract, the exact gap dates, and ask (a) is the internship covered by your student permit, and (b) if not, what documents they'll issue for the extension. Get a written answer. Then send that answer to the hotel's HR so they know the timeline is in motion. Also check your permit card: if it has a 'temporary extension' note, even better.

3f841b34-7da5-4967-a85b-c8e86d534a5a.body:
You've hit the single most frustrating wall for international students in Switzerland, and the first thing to know is: the 'no C permit = rejected' line is common practice, not law. Anti-discrimination rules and cantonal practice technically don't allow regies to categorically refuse based on permit type, but proving that is a fight no student wants, so the realistic strategy is to make your application so strong they can't justify saying no.

1) **Is 'no C permit = rejected' legal?** — There's no legal basis for rejecting solely on permit type. In practice, regies reject B-permit applicants not because of the permit but because they read 'B permit + student' as 'higher risk'. The fix is to neutralise that risk in your dossier, not to argue the law.

2) **Do regies accept bank guarantees instead of a personal guarantor?** — Yes, and this is your strongest card. A 'Garantie bancaire' or a deposit in a Swiss blocked account (Mietkautionskonto) is widely accepted and often preferred to a personal guarantor. A deposit of 2-3 months' rent in a blocked rent-deposit account (via a Swiss bank or even some fintechs now) directly answers the regie's core worry. Offer 3 months' deposit upfront if you can, or ask for the 2-month standard but offer to show the full amount available.

3) **Making a B-permit application stand out** — Beyond the deposit, assemble what regies actually weigh: 3 months of payslips (you have them), the debt enforcement register extract (you have it), a copy of your permit, and crucially *proof of longer-term plans*: a letter from your school confirming your programme length and expected graduation, plus a note that you intend to stay. A longer lease (12+ months) also signals stability — regies love predictability. And yes, offering a slightly higher deposit than requested (within reason) is a legitimate signal.

4) **How other international students solve it** — The most common real-world solutions, in order: (a) co-renting/colocation where one person with a C permit or stable salary signs and you're a named secondary tenant; (b) taking a furnished sublet (sous-location) from an outgoing student — way less documentation, and it builds Swiss rental history; (c) going private landlord via anibis.ch/tutti.ch with a strong dossier and a generous deposit; (d) using a rent deposit guarantee service. None of these is glamorous, but each gets you a roof and a rental reference.

**Practical next step:** build your 'dossier' now even before you apply — debt register extract (free from your canton's office), a school confirmation letter, 3 months of payslips, and proof of a deposit account. Then target private landlords and outgoing-student sublets first, where your dossier + deposit will win; treat regies as the long shot you apply to in parallel.

564d74e3-e9e6-4ae9-a24b-52608f27a5c8.body:
Good news first: paying a reminder fee is annoying, but you have not ruined your credit record. Let me walk you through exactly where the line is.

1) **Is a CHF 10 reminder fee standard and legal?** — Yes, and it's not just legal, it's standard across Swiss billing. Insurers, telecoms, and utilities commonly charge a reminder fee (Mahngebühr) after the due date, usually CHF 5-20. It's part of the contract terms, so it's enforceable. Don't contest it — it's not worth the energy, and it's a normal cost of the slip. Pay it and move on.

2) **When does a missed QR-bill escalate to Betreibung?** — The escalation chain is usually: invoice → reminder (Mahnung) with a fee → second reminder → then a *Betreibung* (debt enforcement). The number of reminders before Betreibung varies by company — some go after two, some after three, and it's typically 30 days past the last reminder. Critically: a Betreibung is not triggered by one late QR-bill. It's triggered by *continued* non-payment after reminders. You paid already, so you've exited the chain at step one.

3) **Does a paid-with-delay bill leave a trace?** — Only the formal Betreibung is visible to third parties (landlords, regies, banks pulling a debt register extract). A reminder fee and a late payment that was settled before Betreibung do NOT appear on the debt enforcement register. So your future rental application is unaffected. The only thing that could bite is if a *second* bill to the same company got left unpaid and escalated — so just don't do that.

4) **Automating QR-bills so this never happens again** — Yes, and it's free or cheap, no premium banking needed: (a) eBill through your bank/PostFinance — insurers, telecoms, and utilities send bills directly to your eBill inbox and you approve in one tap; (b) set up direct debit (LSV/DD) for recurring bills like insurance — approved once, paid automatically; (c) most insurers and utilities now offer automatic QR-bill payment from your account. You can also set a standing order on TWINT for small recurring payments. The combination of eBill + one-tap approval kills the 'forgot the paper bill' failure mode completely.

**Bottom line:** pay the CHF 10, don't stress, set up eBill and direct debit this week, and your credit record is clean.

ef27094d-c680-454d-ace3-e7b4b5a3540f.body:
Your instinct is right: Swiss payroll is lumpy by design, and 'budget monthly' advice from YouTubers who live in countries with monthly salaries doesn't translate. The fix is to budget by year, not by month — and the 13th salary is the perfect illustration of why.

1) **How do students treat the 13th salary?** — The smart move, and what most financially stable students do: treat the 13th as a *planned* payment, not a windfall. Split it in your head: if your rent + insurance + food baseline needs X/month, the two half-payments (June and December are the common schedule) are your buffer months for the big annual costs: annual transport pass, the health insurance franchise you'll pay on a claim, a deposit top-up, or a tuition instalment. If you pre-commit the 13th to the known annual costs, it stops being 'lumpy income' and becomes your annual expense fund.

2) **Budgeting apps for QR-bills and TWINT** — A spreadsheet is honestly fine and many people use one, but there are good Swiss options: **FinanceGuru** (Swiss, syncs your accounts, handles the Swiss specifics), **Anoia/Anorak**, or the built-in budgeting in your bank's app if it's a Swiss bank (Yuh, PostFinance, neon all have spending overviews). The important part isn't the app — it's setting up eBill and direct debits so bills come to one place. For QR-bills specifically, eBill (free, via your bank) shows you the bill, you approve in one tap, done. TWINT is for person-to-person and small shop payments, not really for budgeting.

3) **Asking your landlord to split rent into smaller QR-bills** — Don't. Rent QR-bills are standardised to a monthly schedule and regies/landlords won't split them for one tenant; it looks like you're struggling and can make applications harder. Instead, split *yourself*: keep a dedicated sub-account (most Swiss fintechs let you create a free sub-account) and auto-transfer the rent amount each month so the money is there when the bill arrives.

4) **eBill vs manual QR payment — hidden fees?** — eBill itself is free at Swiss banks (PostFinance, UBS, ZKB, and the fintechs all offer it at no cost). Manual QR payment via your bank's app is also free. The hidden cost is entirely human: manual = you have to remember, and forgetting is what produces the reminder fees. eBill removes that failure mode. So: eBill for everything that supports it, direct debit for the rest, sub-account for rent.

**Practical next step:** open a free sub-account today, set an automatic transfer on payday into it for rent + insurance + a buffer, set up eBill on your main account, and write the 13th salary into your annual cost list before it lands. Your future self will thank you in June.

9bdbe2c4-b5d8-41e9-a87b-a8bfebcff0d9.body:
This is one of the smartest questions a 22-year-old can ask, because most people open a 3a without checking whether they can even use the deduction — and your situation is exactly the case where the answer is nuanced.

1) **Is 3a worth it if Quellensteuer is your final tax?** — Here's the honest math: if you're on Quellensteuer at source and your income is under the threshold where you must file a full tax return, a 3a contribution gives you *no tax deduction now*, because there's no tax return to deduct it against. You'd be locking money in a pillar 3a account purely for the tax-free growth — which is still real (no tax on gains, and you don't pay tax on the withdrawal principal). But if your internship income is small, the growth on a few thousand CHF over 2-3 years is modest, and you can't touch the money easily. So: the tax deduction benefit — the main reason people open 3a — is off the table for you right now.

2) **What do people actually pay withdrawing when they leave?** — This is the part most people discover too late. When you leave Switzerland permanently and withdraw your 3a, the tax is a separate, low rate — generally well below your marginal rate. For a fund/account 3a of a few thousand CHF, the withdrawal tax leaving from Vaud is typically a few percent (a few hundred CHF), and it's computed on the *withdrawal amount*, not the contributions. Leaving from Zurich is similar ballpark. It's not a penalty — it's a small, one-time exit tax, and for small balances it's trivial. The horror stories are about people who let a 3a grow for 30 years and then withdraw a large six-figure sum — then the tax is real.

3) **Should you split between a bank 3a and insurance 3a?** — Not at 22 with low income and uncertain Swiss future. Insurance-based 3a products carry higher costs and penalties in early years (you're essentially locked for 5-10 years with surrender charges). A simple bank 3a (or fintech 3a like those from Yuh/frankly, Viac, or SELV) is flexible — you can pause contributions and it's easy to withdraw when you leave. Split accounts matter only once you're earning real money in Switzerland and maxing contributions. At your stage: one flexible bank 3a, minimal contribution, zero drama.

**My recommendation for you specifically:** if you're unsure about staying, keep your money liquid instead. The best 'Swiss savings' product for a student who may leave is a free account with a sub-account structure (for budgeting) plus, once you're earning and filing taxes, then start 3a. If you want to start anyway, put a small amount (a few hundred CHF/year) in a flexible bank 3a — the tax-free growth is nice-to-have, not the reason to start.

**Practical next step:** decide based on your stay horizon. If you're >70% likely to stay 3+ years and then earn Swiss salary, open a small flexible 3a. If you might leave after your MSc, keep the cash liquid and revisit 3a when you have a Swiss salary and a tax return to deduct against.

9044bad1-5e6b-47bd-a15d-b57235158108.body:
You're asking the exact right question, because the answer determines whether you're double-taxed, refunded, or owed money. Here's how it actually works.

1) **When is Quellensteuer truly final for a B-permit holder?** — Quellensteuer is your final tax if your income is below the threshold that triggers mandatory full assessment. That threshold is set by each canton; in Vaud it's a gross income around CHF 120,000 for a single person (it varies by canton — Zurich is similar, some cantons differ). With an annual gross of ~CHF 24,000, you are *far* below it. So: Quellensteuer is final for you, you do NOT file a Swiss tax return, and you are NOT taxed twice. The withholding IS your tax. Done.

2) **The 13th salary bumping a month's withholding — can it be corrected?** — This is a real quirk. Withholding is calculated per payroll period, so a month where the 13th is paid can indeed show a higher withholding rate for that one month. Here's the good news: at year-end, the cantonal tax office reconciles Quellensteuer for employees, and *over-withholding from the 13th is one of the classic cases that gets refunded*. The mechanism: if your situation warrants it, you (or your employer) can ask for a 'Bezug einer vollen Veranlagung' (voluntary full assessment) — but for CHF 24k income that's usually not worth it. The simpler truth: most cantons' annual reconciliation smooths this out. If after year-end you suspect you overpaid, you can request a refund via the cantonal tax office with your payslips.

3) **Does a partial tax return to claim deductions (like 3a) make sense?** — Yes, and this is the one tool that's genuinely useful for you. Switzerland allows 'voluntary full assessment' — filing a return even when below the threshold — *specifically* so that deductions (pillar 3a contributions, certain expenses) reduce your tax and you get a refund of withheld amounts. If you contribute to 3a or have deductible expenses, a voluntary return can refund you real money. BUT — read this carefully — it only pays off if you have deductions worth claiming. On CHF 24k gross, your refund is modest. It's worth doing only if you're making 3a contributions or have other deductible costs.

**Bottom line:** you are not doing taxes twice. Quellensteuer is final at your income level. The only two moves worth considering: (a) if a 13th-salary month over-withheld, check the canton's reconciliation/refund process after year-end; (b) if you open a 3a, file a voluntary full assessment to reclaim the deduction. Everything else — ignore the tax-return chatter until your gross approaches six figures.

b178ec51-eb94-4ed8-a235-1f6abab7f798.body:
The fintech-vs-bank question is actually simpler than the marketing makes it, and the answer for a student is almost always: fintech now, traditional bank later.

1) **Has anyone had issues getting a salary deposited to a Yuh or neon IBAN?** — Real answer: no, and this fear is mostly an echo of an old concern. Both Yuh (Swissquote + PostFinance JV) and neon (backed by Hypothekarbank Lenzburg) are licensed, provide a proper Swiss IBAN (Yuh gives you a CH IBAN, neon partners with a Swiss bank), and receive salary payments fine. Swiss employers pay to any CH IBAN — they don't care which bank issues it. The 'salary flagged' stories are not about fintech per se; they're about money-laundering checks on unusual inflows, which can happen at any bank. A regular Swiss salary to your own IBAN is completely normal.

2) **Do fintech accounts hurt your mortgage or credit check later?** — Largely no, with one nuance. Swiss credit checks (for mortgages and rental applications) pull the debt enforcement register and, for mortgages, assess your income and existing debts — not which bank you use. Your account history doesn't appear on the register. The nuance: when you apply for a *mortgage*, the bank likes to see a few years of consistent income statements, and having everything in one traditional bank can make the file cleaner. But that's a 'nice for the mortgage application at age 30' consideration, not a reason to pay CHF 10-15/month at 22.

3) **Is there a free tier at a traditional bank?** — Yes, and it's often the best of both worlds. Many Swiss cantonal banks and big banks (e.g. ZKB, Raiffeisen, and others) offer free student packages — free account while you study, sometimes with a free debit card. Some require you to stay a few years after graduation or start charging once you leave the student status. So the optimal move for a student who wants a 'real bank' brand without fees is: get a free student package at a traditional bank *and* use a fintech for day-to-day spending and budgeting. Yuh even offers a free sub-account structure for exactly this.

4) **What's the real cost difference?** — You're looking at ~CHF 0/month for fintech (or ~CHF 5-10 for premium tiers with extra cards/limits) vs CHF 10-15/month for a traditional current account. Over three semesters plus a year of internships, that's roughly CHF 400-600 — real money for a student. The things fintechs lack are mostly irrelevant to you: physical branches (you don't need them), cash deposit machines (neon charges for cash-in, Yuh limited), and large-amount services (not your case).

**Bottom line:** for receiving your internship salary and everyday life, a fintech (Yuh or neon) is the right call and won't hurt your future. If you want the traditional-bank brand for the mortgage-application story later, take a free student package at a traditional bank too — but don't pay for it. And whatever you pick, set up eBill + sub-accounts for budgeting; that's what actually matters.

**Practical next step:** open a Yuh or neon account this week (both have referral bonuses, so ask a friend), set up eBill and a sub-account for rent, and in a few years when you have a real salary, revisit a traditional bank with a free or bundled package.

8ad21232-13c2-47cf-ade6-918fb437aae9.body:
Take a breath — EHL's bachelor is intense, but 'brutal' is mostly survivor-story inflation. The accurate version: it's demanding in a *structured* way, and the students who struggle are usually the ones who don't plan for the structure.

1) **How many hours a week during the heavy semesters?** — Realistic estimate: 40-55 hours of class, projects, and study in the operational semesters (the first-year semesters with La Ruche/F&B practice), plus the group-project load on top. The 'no social life' stories usually come from students who also worked part-time or frontloaded everything. It's comparable to a demanding full-time job plus a side project — survivable, not brutal, if you treat it like a job with fixed hours rather than a free-for-all.

2) **Is the group-project load genuinely as bad as claimed?** — The *volume* is manageable; the *group dynamics* are the real tax. EHL is group-project heavy, and the pain is almost always a teammate who doesn't pull weight or a personality clash. The students who do well learn two skills fast: (a) agreeing on a division of work and a schedule in the first meeting, and (b) documenting everything so free-riders can't sink the project. Treat group work as a professional skill you're learning, because it's genuinely what hotel management careers run on.

3) **Part-time job or extracurricular during term — realistic or a mistake?** — In the light semesters, a small job (10-15h/week) is realistic for many. In the heavy operational semesters, it's a mistake for most. The EHL-friendly pattern: work during lighter semesters and inter-semester breaks, go quiet during the operations-heavy terms. An extracurricular you're committed to is fine and actually looks great on CVs — but pick one, not three.

4) **Do semesters alternate between light and heavy?** — Yes — this is the planning tool you're missing. The EHL bachelor alternates operational/practical semesters (heavy on hours and group work) with more academic ones, and includes internship semesters that take you off campus. Students who plan exchange semesters and internships into the lighter windows, and who frontload the heavy semesters, report a far more manageable ride. Ask current students (or the programme office) for the actual semester-by-semester load map before you set your expectations — it's publicly knowable and it changes everything.

**Bottom line:** expect a serious workload in the operations semesters, budget your energy in the light ones, master the group-work game, and don't take on a job during the heavy terms. That combination is how people survive — and enjoy — EHL.

37bb2098-460f-4b07-aac2-19e6be2258f7.body:
Let me give you the unvarnished picture, because this is where good advice and Swiss reality diverge.

1) **Can you negotiate a first offer?** — Real talk: for a junior/entry F&B position in Switzerland, a first offer is usually take-it-or-leave-it *on base salary*. Swiss hotels operate on fairly standardised scales for entry roles, and there's little flexibility because the salary bands are benchmarked (and often tied to collective labour agreements — the L-GAV in the hotel/gastro sector). What you *can* negotiate is almost everything else: accommodation, meals, uniform allowance, schedule, start date, and — most valuably — a review date. Pushing back on the base for an entry role can genuinely make you look difficult; negotiating the package makes you look professional. If you want to ask for more money, the smart phrasing is 'I'd love to accept — is there flexibility on X?' framed around the package, not 'I want more salary'.

2) **Is CHF 4,200 gross (with 13th) around the norm for a first F&B position near Lac Léman?** — Yes, that's a realistic, slightly-good offer for an entry F&B role in the Vaud/lake Geneva region. Entry F&B salaries in Switzerland generally sit in the CHF 3,800-4,500 gross/month range (before the 13th), with hotels in the big lake cities and five-star properties at the higher end. CHF 4,200 including the 13th is fine for a new grad. For reference, the hotel/gastro sector is on the lower end of Swiss pay generally, which is precisely why the L-GAV and tips matter.

3) **What's take-home after Quellensteuer?** — This is the piece everyone miscalculates. At CHF 4,200 gross/month with the 13th, your Quellensteuer withholding for a single B-permit holder in Vaud is roughly 3-6% (it's a flat-ish withholding table). So expect net around CHF 3,950-4,050/month in a normal month. On the 13th-salary month, the withholding rate can bump up for that one period — and the year-end reconciliation usually smooths it. Also subtract: health insurance (~CHF 250-320 for young adults on a basic plan), rent, and your lifestyle. Take-home of ~CHF 4,000 on a CHF 4,200 gross is a normal, workable Swiss entry salary — tight but liveable, especially with staff meals.

4) **The one lever that matters most** — Don't negotiate the number; negotiate the *review*. Ask for a written 6-month review with the possibility of an increase then. That's how Swiss hospitality careers actually progress, and it costs the hotel nothing today while securing your future raise.

**Practical next step:** accept the base (or negotiate a small package improvement like accommodation/meals), and before signing, ask in writing for: (a) a 6-month salary review, (b) confirmation of the 13th-salary schedule, and (c) any L-GAV extras you're entitled to. Take the job, do it well, and let the review date be your negotiation point.

c8723917-723a-45dd-a88a-6344b718014a.body:
Straight answer: landing a 5-star MT straight out of school is possible but rare, and the people who tell you it's guaranteed are usually selling you something. Here's the realistic playbook.

1) **How realistic is it straight out of school?** — Most of the big names (Four Seasons, Ritz-Carlton, Kempinski, Fairmont) want 6-12 months of operational experience *before* the MT application, and their cohorts are small (5-15 people worldwide). So 'straight out of school with only internships' is an uphill path, but not impossible — what separates the accepted ones is nearly always internship track record and how well they've networked inside the brand, not grades. If you don't land an MT in year one, the standard route is: 6-12 months in an operational role at the target brand, then apply from inside — internally recruited MTs are common.

2) **What does selection actually weigh?** — Ranked roughly in practice: (a) internship experience at the brand or its tier, (b) the panel interviews (they test service mindset and handling pressure more than textbook knowledge), (c) operational references, (d) language skills (English + ideally German/French for Swiss MTs), (e) grades last. The message: your EHL grades help you get the interview, but your internship track record gets you the offer.

3) **Apply through the portal months ahead, or reach out to a specific hotel's HRD?** — Both, in that order. Submit through the group's careers portal early (cohorts fill and close months ahead), *and* separately reach out to a target hotel's HR director after doing an internship there or with a tailored note. Portal alone gets you into the pile; the HRD relationship gets you out of it. The single most effective move: do a summer internship at the specific hotel, perform, and tell the HRD you're applying for the MT — internal recommendation beats external application every time.

4) **How to spot a real MT vs a shift-filler?** — Three tells: (a) a defined rotation schedule across departments with named milestones (not 'you'll move around'), (b) a clear end-state — 'MT graduate → Assistant F&B Manager or Rooms position' — in writing, (c) whether previous MT grads of that programme are actually in management roles today (LinkedIn-check 5 alumni). If the programme can't show you alumni in real management positions, treat it as cheap labour with a fancy title. Also check the compensation and whether rotations are structured across rooms and F&B, or just one department.

**Practical next step:** pick your target brand and hotel now, do a 6-month internship there if possible, and while you're inside, tell the HRD you intend to apply for the MT cohort. Then apply on the portal early. If that door stays shut, take the operational role at the brand and re-apply as an internal candidate — the two-year plan is the realistic one for most people.

bb1e4910-44f3-4e2f-addf-41de300427c2.body:
Short answer: for a fresh hospitality grad job-hunting in Switzerland, LinkedIn Premium is a *maybe*, not a must-have — and most of the features people cite are either free or don't matter for hospitality recruiting.

1) **Has Premium actually gotten anyone an interview?** — Honestly: rarely, and the studies/echoes on this are consistent. Recruiters for Swiss hotels post jobs, browse candidates, and message them through free LinkedIn. InMail is the feature Premium sells hardest, but in hospitality specifically, recruiters commonly respond to free connection requests with a short note anyway. The people who genuinely benefit from Premium are in high-volume, high-competition corporate recruiting pipelines, not hotel entry roles. For hospitality, your job hunt success is driven by the network you already have (internship contacts, alumni, campus recruiters), not by InMail credits.

2) **Does Premium make you look desperate?** — No. Nobody can see that you have Premium (your badge is only visible if you turn it on, and almost nobody cares). Recruiters see 'Open to Work' and your profile, full stop. So there's no stigma to worry about — the question is purely whether it's worth the money.

3) **What's actually useful about Premium for you?** — The one genuinely useful feature is 'Who Viewed Your Profile' — but its real value isn't vanity; it's learning which recruiter profiles are looking at you so you can reach out first. The other useful piece is being able to see full profile info of people outside your network (e.g. a hotel's HRD you want to contact) — though most Swiss hotel people have open profiles. And the extra InMail allowance matters only if you're cold-pitching a lot of people without any connection.

4) **Money better spent elsewhere?** — Almost certainly, for you. For the price of 1-2 months of Premium you could: buy a professional CV/cover-letter review (often CHF 50-150) tailored to Swiss hospitality, get a photography session for your profile, or take a short certification that shows on your profile. Those have a higher ROI for a Swiss hotel job hunt than Premium. And the free version of LinkedIn already gives you job alerts, Open to Work, and connection requests — the core search machinery.

**Bottom line:** take the free trial if you want to test it (and if you do, set a calendar reminder to cancel before the charge — the trial auto-renews at full price). Use it for the 'Who Viewed' intel during your active hunt, then cancel. Spend your real money on a CV review and a good profile photo instead.

**Practical next step:** activate 'Open to Work' (recruiters-only visibility), polish your headline with your target role and location ('Hospitality Graduate | F&B | Lausanne'), and use the free tier to connect with HRDs at your target hotels. If you want the visibility intel for a month, trial Premium — but cancel on day 28.

87e51143-a5f9-42ad-a7c8-352807670cfd.body:
The conflicting advice you're getting is because there are *two different audiences* for a CV in Switzerland: the ATS filter and the human recruiter. The trick is satisfying both at once, and it's very doable.

1) **Photo, DOB, nationality — include or skip?** — Human recruiters in Switzerland (and German-speaking Europe generally) still *expect* a professional photo, and many Swiss HR managers find a photo-less CV slightly unusual — the photo is conventional, not optional, in Swiss hospitality. That said, an ATS scanner doesn't care about the photo, and DOB/nationality are legally sensitive in some countries' ATS systems. The Swiss compromise that works: include a clean professional photo (it's expected), include nationality and work-permit status (B/L permit) *briefly* because Swiss HR genuinely needs to know your permit situation, but skip DOB — it adds nothing and invites irrelevant scrutiny. Some big-chain portals explicitly ask for permit status separately anyway.

2) **Europass — avoid it?** — Yes, avoid it. Europass templates are widely disliked by Swiss recruiters because they're bloated and non-standard. Swiss hospitality HR wants a clean, one-page CV, standard chronological structure, tailored to the specific hotel and role.

3) **One page or two for a new grad?** — One page, definitively. A new grad has one page of relevant content; a two-page CV at your stage reads as padding. The only exception is if the role requires listing languages, permits, and a full education history — then a tight second page is acceptable. For almost everyone in your position: one page.

4) **Cover letter in the local language — dealbreaker?** — This is the big one, and the honest answer is: German or French *matters* at Swiss hotels, but B1 can be enough if you're honest about it. The single most effective move: write the cover letter in the local language (German for Zurich region, French for Vaud/Geneva) even with imperfect grammar — a short, clear letter in the local language signals commitment and beats a flawless English letter. If your German is genuinely B1, keep the letter short (5-6 sentences), state your level honestly, and put 'Deutsch B1, Französisch A2, English C2' in your language section. Swiss HR values honest self-assessment over a misleading 'fluent' claim that fails in an interview. Also: the cover letter is *not* a dealbreaker at big-chain portals (which often ignore it), but it absolutely helps when you apply directly by email.

5) **ATS-heavy portals vs direct email?** — Both, and this matters. Big-chain portals (e.g. Accor's careers site) are ATS-driven: your CV gets parsed, so keep it simple — one column, standard section headings (Experience, Education, Skills), no tables/graphics/columns, standard fonts, PDF *and* DOCX versions. Many portals reject PDFs or mangle them; provide the .docx they request. In parallel, direct-email applications to smaller hotels (private, independent, or boutique) with a tailored CV + local-language letter often bypass the ATS entirely and land on a human's desk — and hospitality is small enough that a well-crafted direct email to the HRD or GM frequently gets read.

**Practical next step:** build one clean, one-page, ATS-safe CV (no tables, no graphics, standard headings, photo top-left, permit + language line, DOCX + PDF versions) with a tailored one-page cover letter in the local language, and send both formats through portals and direct emails in parallel. The same CV format that passes the ATS also reads well to humans — you don't need two versions, just one disciplined one.
